title: The Stingy Seth (हिन्दी)
summary: A miserly merchant buries his gold coins under a tree and weeps when a thief replaces them with a stone. Birbal reveals that unused wealth has no value. [HI]
full_text:
In the commercial quarters of Agra lived a fabulously wealthy merchant named Seth Chunilal, whose miserliness was legendary. Though he owned three spice warehouses, he wore patched rags, ate watered lentil soup, and never spent a single dam on his wife or children.

Every month, Chunilal converted his profits into heavy gold mohurs, walked secretly into the forest at midnight, and buried the gold in a brass pot beneath an ancient neem tree. Every Sunday night, he crept into the woods, dug up the pot, counted the coins one by one, caressed their smooth golden surfaces, buried them again, and returned home with a sigh of bliss.

One night, a clever thief observed the miser's midnight ritual from behind the bushes. As soon as Chunilal departed, the thief dug up the pot, emptied all one thousand gold mohurs into his sack, filled the pot with heavy river stones, buried it back in the pit, and disappeared.

The following Sunday, Chunilal dug up the pot. He opened the lid, expecting the gleam of gold, but found only grey, cold stones!

The miser let out a shriek that woke the owls. He tore his robes, beat his chest, rolled in the dirt, and wept inconsolably.

Birbal, who was returning from an inspection of the river outpost, came upon the weeping merchant.

'What has happened, Chunilal?' Birbal inquired kindly.

Chunilal sobbed: 'I am ruined, Raja Birbal! A thousand gold coins, my entire life's treasure, stolen from under this tree! Now there is nothing left but these worthless stones!'

Birbal looked at the pit, then at the weeping miser:

'Tell me, Chunilal—did you ever spend any of that gold? Did you buy food for your children, medicine for your wife, or clothes for yourself?'

'Never!' the miser cried. 'I never touched a single coin! I only dug them up once a week to look at them!'

Birbal smiled gently, picked up one of the heavy river stones, and placed it back into the pot:

'Then bury these stones again, Chunilal, and come visit them every Sunday night to look at them! For since you never spent your gold or used it to do good in the world, a pot full of gold coins and a pot full of river stones served exactly the same purpose in your life!'

Chunilal stared at the stones in stunned silence. The truth of Birbal's words pierced through his greed like a sunbeam through fog. Realizing the folly of hoarding what he never enjoyed, the merchant repented and resolved to use his remaining earnings to help the needy.
